statement:
Show that
$$\tan3\theta=\frac{3\tan\theta-\tan^3\theta}{1-3\tan^2\theta}.$$

Given that $\theta=\cos^{-1}(2/\sqrt5)$ and $0<\theta<\pi/2$, show that $\tan3\theta=11/2$.

Hence, or otherwise, find all solutions of the equations

(i) $\tan(3\cos^{-1}x)=11/2$;

(ii) $\cos\left(\tfrac13\tan^{-1}y\right)=2/\sqrt5$.
solution:
Using the double-angle formula for $\tan$,
$$\tan2\theta=\frac{2\tan\theta}{1-\tan^2\theta},$$
and then
$$\tan3\theta=\tan(2\theta+\theta)=\frac{\tan2\theta+\tan\theta}{1-\tan2\theta\tan\theta}=\frac{3\tan\theta-\tan^3\theta}{1-3\tan^2\theta}.$$

For $\theta=\cos^{-1}(2/\sqrt5)$, we have $\cos\theta=2/\sqrt5$ and $\sin\theta=1/\sqrt5$ (as $0<\theta<\pi/2$), so $\tan\theta=\tfrac12$. Hence
$$\tan3\theta=\frac{3(\tfrac12)-(\tfrac12)^3}{1-3(\tfrac12)^2}=\frac{\tfrac32-\tfrac18}{1-\tfrac34}=\frac{\tfrac{11}{8}}{\tfrac14}=\frac{11}{2}.$$

(i) Let $\phi=\cos^{-1}x\in[0,\pi]$. We need $\tan3\phi=11/2$. Since $\tan3\phi=\tan3\theta$ where $\theta=\cos^{-1}(2/\sqrt5)$, we have $3\phi=3\theta+k\pi$, i.e. $\phi=\theta+\tfrac{k\pi}{3}$ for integers $k$ with $0\le\phi\le\pi$, giving $k=0,1,2$.

Thus the solutions are $x=\cos\theta$, $\cos(\theta+\tfrac\pi3)$, $\cos(\theta+\tfrac{2\pi}{3})$. Using $\cos\theta=\tfrac2{\sqrt5}$, $\sin\theta=\tfrac1{\sqrt5}$:
$$x=\frac{2}{\sqrt5},\qquad \frac{2-\sqrt3}{2\sqrt5},\qquad \frac{-2-\sqrt3}{2\sqrt5}.$$

(ii) Let $\psi=\tfrac13\tan^{-1}y$, so $\cos\psi=2/\sqrt5$. Since $\tan^{-1}y\in(-\tfrac\pi2,\tfrac\pi2)$, we have $\psi\in(-\tfrac\pi6,\tfrac\pi6)$, and $\cos\psi=2/\sqrt5$ gives $\psi=\pm\theta$ (as $\cos$ is even). So $\tan^{-1}y=\pm3\theta$, and since $\tan3\theta=11/2$,
$$y=\tan(\pm3\theta)=\pm\frac{11}{2}.$$
hints: Derive tan 3θ from the double-angle formula.
For θ=cos⁻¹(2/√5), find tan θ = 1/2, then tan 3θ = 11/2.
Use the period of tan (period π) and the evenness of cos to find all solutions.
